newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Norwegian minister threatens Afghan aid cut. [CORRECTED 13:02 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Norwegian minister threatens Afghan aid cut. [CORRECTED 13:02 GMT]

text.p: The next chairman of a meeting of donors to Afghanistan said on Thursday he would not recommend aid increases for some sectors if the Taleban are not willing to bring their policies into line with international norms of human rights.

Norwegian Deputy Foreign Minister (Corrects from "Secretary of State") Jan Egeland was speaking at the end of a 24-hour visit to the Afghan capital, where he met Taleban officials and visited aid projects in the city. Egeland is the most senior Western official to visit Kabul since the Taleban took the city last September.
Norway has contributed nearly $200 million to Afghanistan over the last 18 years, making it one of the largest donors of humanitarian aid to the country.

"We feel it is important to be frank and open regarding worries we have about disturbing tendencies of Taleban rule. We fear that the positive image that the Taleban won from providing security is being lost for a number of reasons, including the increasingly strict interpretation on a number of issues we feel contradictory to human rights.

"The number of schools for girls and very restricted professional rights for women is not only a violation of human rights, but also prevents the solidarity of the international community," said Egeland.
When the Taleban took Kabul they closed girls' schools and banned women from working except in the medical sector.
Egeland said that the Taleban deputy foreign minister had agreed to recommend the establishment of a joint commission to promote education across the board.

"The deputy foreign minister agreed after some hesitation that he would recommend a joint commission between the ministry and our professionals to plan and build schools for girls and expand education for boys," said Egeland.
He said that Norway was willing to provide the money for 10 schools immediately if the Taleban could guarantee that boys and girls would have equal access.

But Egeland, who will chair the next meeting of international aid donors to Afghanistan in October, said that he would not recommend any extra funding unless there was progress towards equality in the coming weeks.

"I said (to the Taleban) that unless we see substantial progress in the weeks to come, I would not be recommending to other donors to increase assistance in fields such as education. We would have to seriously reconsider assistance in many other areas." he said.
But he said that he was not trying to use aid funding as a threat to change Taleban policies.
"We should not use funding as a threat, but we must be firm. For example, we will not fund schools unless we can see that they are in conformity with our rules.
"We cannot start long-term development programmes unless we feel that their policies are in conformity with international human rights," said Egeland.

Aid programmes in Afghanistan are already facing a funding crisis. The consolidated appeal for 1997 has received $34 million of a total request for $133 million. The mine clearance programme will run out of money in mid-September unless more money is forthcoming.
Egeland said that he would recommend that aid donors who cut their contributions raise them again.

"Among things I will certainly be recommending will be that donors who cut funding raise it again, and we will consider additional funding ourselves. Demining is the single most important funding requirement in Afghanistan today," he said.
